_label: Fun facts, all from cited Wikipedia articles (accessed 2026-10-11). Uniform numbers for retired players are from Wikipedia's List of Major League Baseball retired numbers.

timeline: AL charter franchise - spent its first season as the Milwaukee Brewers.
St. Louis Browns. Won the franchise's only St. Louis pennant in 1944 (lost the World Series to the Cardinals).
Sold to a Baltimore group led by Clarence Miles and Mayor Thomas D'Alesandro Jr.; became the Baltimore Orioles.
First World Series title - a four-game sweep of the heavily favored Dodgers.
Won the first-ever ALCS.
Second World Series title.
Third World Series title - last of six World Series trips from 1966 to 1983.
Lost the first 21 games of the season.
The 'Why Not?' Orioles finish second in the AL East.
Oriole Park at Camden Yards opens, kicking off the 'retro' ballpark era.
14 straight losing seasons.
Beat Texas in the first AL Wild Card Game.
AL East title and first ALCS trip in 17 years (Buck Showalter / Dan Duquette).
115 losses, most in franchise history.
101-61 and AL East champions, two years after a 52-110 season - led by Rutschman, Henderson, Bautista and Bradish.
David Rubenstein's group buys the club from the Angelos family; wild-card berth.
history.rivalry: AL East rivals - historically the Yankees, more recently the Blue Jays. Regional 'Beltway Series' with the Washington Nationals (Baltimore leads 55-39 per Wikipedia). Club policy: numbers are retired only for Hall of Famers, with Cal Ripken Jr. the lone exception.

uniforms.source_name: Wikipedia - Baltimore Orioles: Logos and uniforms
timeline: First Baltimore uniforms; 'Orioles' script rendered in black with orange trim. Full-bodied bird caps (1954-65).
Home 'Orioles' in block letters instead of script; a black cap with an orange block 'B' was worn for part of 1963.
The 'cartoon bird' cap logo debuts (used until 1988). Player names added to uniforms.
Sleeveless home alternates.
First orange alternate uniforms (with orange pants), lasted two seasons.
Orange pullover alternate; white-paneled black cap with orange brim introduced.
Full-bodied bird returns on an all-black cap.
Black alternate jerseys first worn - still in use (current trim style since 2000).
Script "O's" alternate cap introduced.
'Baltimore' returns to road jerseys after a long fan campaign (road jerseys bore the team name 1973-2008).
Modernized cartoon bird returns; orange alternates return (Saturdays).
Beat the #1-seeded Cardinals to win league feed's 'Battle of the Uniforms' as a #13 seed.
First City Connect: black base, 'BALTIMORE' in white, neighborhood-inspired colors on collar and sleeves.
First jersey sponsor: T. Rowe Price sleeve patch (debuted June 11).
All-orange alternate brought back for select games.
Second City Connect: cream base, 'BMORE' in dark green, Eutaw Street plaque-inspired sleeve patch ('From the stoop to the Yards', '410'); new script 'B' alternate cap.

park.dims_note: Field size per Wikipedia infobox (current configuration; left field was reworked in 2022, and Elias announced further left-field changes in 2024 (wall brought in to 363 ft) - verify against current club signage).
facts: April 6, 1992 - Rick Sutcliffe's complete-game shutout, 2-0 over Cleveland, before a sellout of 44,568.
First of the 'retro' ballparks; credited with starting the wave of neotraditional parks after the cookie-cutter era.
Built on the old B&O Railroad Camden Station rail yard; the former B&O Warehouse dominates the view beyond right field.
Closed to traffic between the park and the warehouse; bronze baseball plaques mark where home runs landed. Boog Powell's barbecue stand is here.
Every seat is green except one orange seat in right field marking Eddie Murray's 500th home run.
Two-tiered bullpen design, a first in the majors, based on public write-in ideas. Bronze statues of the six retired-number greats stand behind them.
Statue of Babe Ruth by Susan Luery (1996) outside the park.
First MLB park since Ebbets Field with an outfield wall made only of straight segments. Field is 16 ft below street level.
GM Mike Elias moved the left-field wall back up to 26.5 ft and raised it from 7 ft to about 13 ft to cut home runs.
Splash zone added in left field in 2023, where 'Mr. Splash' hoses fans after Orioles extra-base hits.
US$110 million to build (1992); taxpayers have covered at least $1.3 billion of stadium costs since 1989.
